To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the analog implementation of a Leaky Integrate and Fire neuron is 5x smaller in area, 20x less energy hungry, and has the same level of precision (in terms of SNR) as the digital implementation.
the digital neuron design is 5 times larger in area than the analog neuron design, while it is 20 times less power efficient than the analog neuron.

the analog implementation of the Leaky Integrate and Fire (LIF) neuron is 5 times more area-efficient and 20 times more energy-efficient than the digital implementation, when both designs achieve the same level of accuracy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of analog and digital hardware spiking neuron models, and the comparison of their respective performances.
the design, simulation, implementation and testing of a novel, highly efficient analog spiking neuron circuit.
the design, analysis and evaluation of a new generation of spiking neuron models that are suitable for implementation in hardware, with a focus on analog VLSI circuits.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

analog designs are the most promising for large-scale silicon spiking neural systems, and digital designs are only useful when analog designs are impossible to implement, such as for very low supply voltages.
the analog neuron is a more efficient design for the implementation of spiking neural networks in silicon.
analog neurons are better than digital ones in terms of area, energy, and speed, and therefore, should be the preferred choice for future silicon neural systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the analog neuron design is a serious competitor to the digital design, in terms of area, power and performance, for large-scale silicon neural networks.

the energy efficiency and area of a spiking neuron is a function of the number of transistors and their sizes in the circuit, which are in turn determined by the performance requirements (SNR, maximum spiking rate) and the technology node.
the analog neuron is the best option for large-scale neuromorphic circuits, and that digital neurons can be used for small-scale applications.
The main takeaway from our work is that
analog neurons can be designed with a similar level of performance and energy efficiency as digital neurons, but at the cost of increased complexity.
the analog approach is not only more energy efficient, but also more compact.
the design complexity of analog circuits can be significantly reduced by using a digital design flow.
